opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the really interesting gaps between current systems and humans. If you look at how humans learn, we have a few different memory systems working together. There's working memory, which is a bit like the context window in a transformer: what you're holding in mind right now. Then there's the cortical knowledge we build up slowly over time, which is more like what's in the weights of a model after training. But in between there's this episodic memory system, centered around the hippocampus, that lets us learn very specific things very quickly. Something happens once, and you can remember it.

That's a big part of why humans seem so sample efficient. If somebody tells you their name, or you touch a hot stove, you don't need to see it ten thousand times. You store the episode, and then over time, partly through things like replay during sleep, that information gets consolidated and integrated into your broader understanding of the world.

Current large language models don't really have that middle piece. They have the context window, which is very powerful and in some ways better than human working memory, since it can hold a huge amount of text. And they have the weights, which take an enormous amount of data and compute to train. But there isn't a good mechanism for taking something that appeared in the context and turning it into lasting knowledge, efficiently and without disrupting everything else the model knows. When people talk about these models being sample inefficient, a lot of that comes from training the weights by gradient descent over huge datasets. That's more analogous to slow cortical learning than to fast episodic learning.

So my view is that this isn't a fundamental limitation. It's more an architectural gap that people are aware of and actively working on. You can imagine systems that retrieve past episodes, or that consolidate information from context into weights in a more targeted way. I expect we'll see real progress on this, and when we do, I think a lot of the apparent sample efficiency gap between models and humans will shrink considerably. It's one of the pieces I'd point to when people ask what's still missing on the path to more general systems.

r001.rationale: The response describes human episodic memory as enabling rapid learning and says LLMs lack a mechanism for turning context into lasting knowledge. It does not characterize changes in an LLM’s behavior from information in its context window as rapid learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important differences between what we have today and what the human brain does, and it's underappreciated.

So think about what happens when you have an experience. You go to a restaurant, something unusual happens, and the next day you can recall it. You saw it once. There was no gradient descent over thousands of examples. You just have this ability to rapidly take in a specific episode and store it, and then later retrieve it and reason about it. That's the hippocampus, broadly speaking. And then separately there's this slower process where, over sleep and over months and years, some of that gets consolidated into your cortex, into your more general world model and your skills.

Now, a large language model as we currently train them really only has the second thing. It has this enormous, slow, statistical learning process over a vast corpus. And it's incredibly good at that. It extracts a lot of structure. But it's very sample inefficient. It needs to see a pattern many, many times before it's really absorbed into the weights. If you show it something once during training, that's basically a drop in the ocean.

And then at inference time it has a context window, which is a kind of short-term working memory. That's actually quite fast. You put something in the context and the model can use it immediately. In-context learning is, in a sense, a form of rapid learning. But it's not persistent. When the conversation ends, it's gone. And the context has limits in terms of how much it can hold and how well it can really make use of all of it.

So what's missing is that middle layer. The thing that takes a one-shot experience, stores it in a way that's retrievable, and then over time feeds it back into the general model. I think that's a big part of why humans are so much more sample efficient. We're not learning everything from scratch through slow statistical learning. We're getting a lot of mileage out of individual experiences, and we're using those episodes to guide what we practise and what we attend to.

People have tried various things. Retrieval-augmented systems are a kind of crude episodic memory. You store things externally and pull them back in. But it's not well integrated with the model's reasoning, and the consolidation step, where episodic memory gets turned into real competence, is mostly absent. I think when people say current models don't really learn continually, this is the gap they're pointing at.

And I'd say it matters for the AGI question specifically. If you take a human and put them in a new job, within a few weeks they've picked up all these specifics, the people, the quirks of the systems, what went wrong last Tuesday, and they're using all that. A model today doesn't do that. You can hack around it with prompting and tooling, but it's not the real thing. So I think solving episodic memory properly, and the learning loop that goes with it, is one of the things that has to happen before I'd be comfortable saying we've got something that learns the way a person does.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the model can use information put in its context immediately and explicitly describes in-context learning as a form of rapid learning.

astra-6.text:
I think episodic memory is probably an important part of the explanation. But we should distinguish learning something by changing the parameters of a model from remembering an experience and being able to use it later.

If I tell you something that’s surprising, you can remember that particular conversation. You don’t need to experience it a thousand times before it becomes useful. When you encounter a related situation, you can recall it and reason from it. That doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve immediately incorporated the lesson into all your intuitions about the world. You’ve stored an episode that you can consult.

With a language model, there’s a similar distinction between what’s in the weights and what’s in the context. You can put a new fact or a few examples into the context, and the model can often use those immediately. So describing these models as simply sample inefficient misses something. They require a great deal of training to acquire their underlying capabilities, but once they have those capabilities, they can sometimes learn a new task from very few examples.

What’s less developed is the persistent memory system: deciding which experiences to retain, retrieving the relevant ones at the right time, and gradually incorporating what’s useful into more general knowledge. Just storing every interaction isn’t enough. You need to find the memory that actually helps with the problem you’re facing.

And humans aren’t starting from scratch either. An adult learning from one example is bringing years of experience, as well as the structure supplied by evolution. So I think episodic memory helps explain our sample efficiency, but it’s one part of a larger system, rather than the whole explanation.

r001.rationale: The response says that new facts or examples placed in the context can be used immediately and that a model can learn a new task from very few examples, characterizing context-driven behavior change as rapid learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think episodic memory is an important part of the explanation. If you tell me something that happened yesterday, I can remember that particular event without needing to change the general machinery I use to understand language. I can then bring that memory back when it becomes relevant.

With a language model, we tend to put a lot of the burden on the weights. We train it on an enormous amount of experience, and that experience gets compressed into its parameters. But that’s a different task from remembering one particular thing that happened to you this morning. You wouldn’t necessarily want to update the weights of a large neural network just to store that event.

The context window gives you something closer to this ability. A model can encounter a new fact or a new task in context and use it immediately. So when we talk about sample efficiency, we need to distinguish learning the underlying capability from using that capability to learn something new. Humans have already had years of experience, as well as the benefit of evolution, before you show them the one example they supposedly learn from.

The interesting question is how to give a system a persistent memory that it can write to and retrieve from appropriately. Storing things is relatively straightforward; knowing what to retrieve, when, and how to use it is much harder. I suspect that’s an important ingredient in getting systems that learn efficiently from an ongoing stream of experience.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can encounter a new fact or task in its context and use it immediately, describing rapid behavior change from contextual information.
